Pulmonary Disorders

Tuberculosis

Tuberculosis is both a clinical diagnosis problem and a public-health problem. ED care starts before confirmatory cultures return: recognize risk, isolate suspected active disease, collect appropriate tests, and coordinate public-health follow-up.

Isolation trap: suspected active pulmonary TB belongs in airborne isolation while evaluation proceeds; a negative PPD, IGRA, smear, or NAAT alone must not falsely reassure you.

TUBERCULOSIS

INTRODUCTION AND EPIDEMIOLOGY

TB remains a major worldwide infection and a leading infectious killer, especially in patients with HIV and in populations with limited access to screening and treatment. In the ED, risk recognition includes birth or residence in high-prevalence countries, HIV, homelessness or shelter exposure, incarceration, injection drug use, nursing home residence, older age, and close contact with infectious TB.

Tintinalli frames TB as a pulmonary-disorders chapter, but Rosen emphasizes the ED as a front-line public-health entry point. Missed isolation and missed reporting can expose other patients, staff, and household contacts.

PATHOPHYSIOLOGY

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a slow-growing aerobic rod transmitted by inhaled droplet nuclei. It favors high-oxygen and high-blood-flow areas. Only some exposed persons become infected, and only some infected persons progress to active disease.

PRIMARY AND LATENT INFECTION

After inhalation, host cell-mediated immunity may contain the organism in granulomas. Tubercules may caseate and calcify; the Ghon complex is a classic calcified pulmonary focus with hilar lymph nodes. Latent infection is not transmissible, but it is a reservoir for future reactivation. The skin test usually becomes positive 1 to 2 months after exposure.

Tintinalli source

Figure 67-1

Primary ghon complex.

REACTIVATION TUBERCULOSIS

Reactivation occurs when immunity can no longer contain dormant foci. Risk rises with HIV, older age, solid-organ cancer, leukemia, transplant, TNF-alpha antagonists, prolonged corticosteroids, diabetes, renal failure requiring hemodialysis, psoriasis, and silicosis. In HIV, progression to active disease can occur rapidly and repeatedly.

CLINICAL FEATURES

PRIMARY TUBERCULOSIS

Primary infection is often asymptomatic and detected by screening or imaging. Active primary TB may cause cough, fever, malaise, weight loss, chest pain, pneumonitis-like illness, and hilar adenopathy. Immunocompromised patients can deteriorate rapidly even when early findings are subtle.

REACTIVATION TUBERCULOSIS

Reactivation can be systemic, pulmonary, or extrapulmonary. Fever, night sweats, malaise, fatigue, weight loss, productive cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, and pleuritic chest pain are classic. Symptoms may be chronic and vague; physical exam can be unremarkable. Extrapulmonary TB can mimic many common diseases, especially in elderly and HIV patients.

DIAGNOSIS AND DIFFERENTIAL DIAGNOSIS

In ED patients with undiagnosed TB, classic pulmonary disease is often not considered until late. Suspect TB in any patient older than 50 with pneumonia-like presentation or prominent respiratory complaint, especially if treatment has failed, exposure risk exists, or immune compromise is present. Place possible TB patients in a separate area and use high-efficiency masks/respiratory protection while awaiting results.

MANTOUX OR TUBERCULIN SKIN TEST

The Mantoux test uses intradermal purified protein derivative and is read at 48 to 72 hours. Interpretation depends on risk group and induration size. A negative skin test does not rule out active TB; approximately 20% of active TB patients may test negative. False negatives occur with immunosuppression, recent infection, severe illness, and recent live-virus vaccination; false positives may occur with BCG or nontuberculous mycobacteria.

Table 67-2

Interpretation of purified protein derivative skin test.

BLOOD TESTS

IGRAs assess interferon-gamma response to TB antigens and are useful for latent TB screening, especially when follow-up for skin test reading is unreliable or BCG confounds PPD interpretation. IGRA cannot distinguish latent from active infection and should not be used to exclude active TB.

CHEST RADIOGRAPH

Chest radiography supports evaluation after symptoms or positive screening. Primary TB can have normal x-ray, parenchymal infiltrate, hilar or mediastinal adenopathy, calcified nodes, or unilateral pleural effusion. Reactivation usually favors the upper lobe or superior lower-lobe segments and may show cavitation, fibrosis, scarring, or calcification. HIV and immunocompromised patients may have atypical or normal radiographs.

MICROSCOPY AND CULTURES

Sputum culture remains the best confirmatory method, but culture takes time. Smear microscopy is rapid but insensitive; a negative smear does not exclude TB. NAAT can return quickly and detect MTB DNA and resistance markers, but false positives and false negatives occur. Positive smear plus positive NAAT should trigger treatment while cultures are pending; negative NAAT cannot exclude TB.

TREATMENT

TREATMENT OF ACTIVE TUBERCULOSIS

Active TB requires multidrug therapy to overcome resistance. Standard initial therapy uses isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol in an intensive phase followed by continuation therapy based on culture and susceptibility results. Most EDs do not start TB medications independently; initiation should be coordinated with infectious disease/public health unless the case is classic and follow-up is secured.

Tintinalli source

Table 67-3

Adult treatment of tuberculosis.

Monitor for hepatotoxicity, optic neuritis, neuropathy, hyperuricemia, drug interactions, and adherence barriers. Directly observed therapy is central when compliance is uncertain. Fixed drug combinations can reduce relapse and secondary resistance.

TREATMENT OF LATENT TUBERCULOSIS

Latent treatment is for recent converters, close contacts of active TB, and anergic patients with known contact. INH-based therapy reduces conversion risk, with rifamycin-based alternatives when indicated. Latent therapy decisions still need follow-up systems; the ED should not create a prescription without a plan.

DISPOSITION AND FOLLOW-UP

OUTPATIENT CARE

Many TB patients start therapy as outpatients, but safe discharge requires public-health coordination, long-term follow-up, home isolation instructions, and reporting. Suspected or confirmed TB should be reported promptly to public health, often within 24 hours depending jurisdiction. Discharge without a public-health handoff is a systems failure.

HOSPITAL ADMISSION

Admit ill-appearing, hypoxemic, or dyspneic patients; uncertain diagnoses; patients with likely nonadherence or unsafe social situations; and patients with suspected active drug-resistant TB. Hospitalized suspected TB patients need respiratory isolation, ideally negative-pressure rooms, and contact tracing. Engineering controls and respirator use are part of treatment because they prevent the next case.

SPECIAL POPULATIONS

PATIENTS WITH TUBERCULOSIS AND HUMAN IMMUNODEFICIENCY VIRUS

HIV is the strongest known risk factor for TB, and TB may define acquired immunodeficiency syndrome. HIV patients may have atypical radiographs, extrapulmonary disease, and drug interactions, especially with rifampin and antiretrovirals. Consider HIV testing when TB is suspected because early diagnosis changes therapy and public-health risk.

MULTIDRUG-RESISTANT TUBERCULOSIS

MDR-TB means resistance at least to INH and rifampin. Risk factors include prior unsuccessful treatment, poor adherence, HIV, injection drug use, close contact with source cases, high-resistance travel or origin, cavitary disease, homelessness, imprisonment, and malabsorption. MDR-TB requires specialist consultation and rapid isolation; standard first-line assumptions may fail.

CHILDREN

Children often have subtle disease, lower sputum yield, and more lymphadenitis. Primary infection can be asymptomatic or present with fever, night sweats, cough, poor feeding, and fatigue. Diagnosis frequently depends on contact tracing, TST/IGRA, imaging, and clinical judgment.

MILIARY TUBERCULOSIS

Miliary TB reflects hematogenous dissemination with many small lesions and can present with fever, anorexia, night sweats, cough, weight loss, splenomegaly, hepatomegaly, lymphadenopathy, and severe respiratory failure. The classic miliary pattern may not appear until disease is advanced.

EXTRAPULMONARY TUBERCULOSIS

Extrapulmonary TB involves lymphatic, pleural, bone/joint, genitourinary, meningeal, peritoneal, and other sites. It is more common with HIV and in children. Symptoms depend on site, and pulmonary imaging can be normal.

TUBERCULOUS MENINGITIS

Tuberculous meningitis causes fever, headache, cognitive change, cranial nerve palsies, focal deficits, or hydrocephalus. CSF often shows lymphocytic pleocytosis, high protein, and low glucose. Treatment is prolonged and adjunctive corticosteroids reduce complications.
